articles.title: Persisting fault lines
articles.content: HISTORY, it has famously been said, repeats itself first as tragedy and then as farce. Today, it is repeating itself in Pakistan as both tragedy and farce. Recent events have deepened some of the country’s overlapping fault lines — enduring features that have shaped its political landscape for decades. Together they have contributed to its chronic instability and impeded its progress. It has meant the absence of a calm and predictable environment in which to meet the country’s growing challenges. The country seems caught in a time warp with a power elite ensuring it cannot escape its past. Four fault lines (there are others too) are laid bare by recent political developments: unceasing confrontation between the government and opposition; centre-province conflict resulting in dismissal of elected provincial governments; parliament’s marginal role in the political system; and weak institutions whose evolution is stymied or independence eroded by predatory ruling elites. The ongoing confrontation between the PML-N-led government and PTI may have novel aspects but it reflects a long-standing fault line in the country’s divisive politics. Government-opposition conflicts have been endemic in Pakistan’s history, with political behaviour driven by the ethic of war rather than competition. Political leaders and parties have viewed opponents as enemies to be eliminated from the political arena in a terminal conflict, not rivals to compete with, much less accommodated. Branding opponents as disloyal to the country is a well-worn, unseemly tradition. This is evident today by the disingenuous narrative peddled by federal ministers that the ousted KP government was aligned with terrorist organisations. A culture of compromise, tolerance, and restraint never took root leaving ruling and opposition parties perpetually at loggerheads. This, in turn, opened the door to both direct and indirect interventions by the military, which could always count on support from one political party or another to oust governments and expand its power. Divide and rule strategies pursued by the establishment also fuelled political conflict. Some enduring aspects of the political landscape are holding Pakistan back. There were rare moments of political consensus as for example when the 1973 Constitution was adopted, Charter of Democracy agreed (but never implemented) between Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif in 2006 and in more recent years, the unanimous passage of the 18th Constitutional Amendment in 2010. Beyond these and some other exceptions, the tradition of intolerance and authoritarian behaviour has persisted. Opposition parties have rarely accepted the legitimacy of governments while governments refused to recognise opposition as a legitimate activity fundamental to democracy. The underlying reason has usually been disputed elections. Pakistan’s history is replete with losing sides contesting results and alleging ballot fraud, often for good reason. This happened most recently in the 2024 election which, despite its controversial nature, still saw PTI winning a plurality in the national legislature. It was blocked from forming the federal government by an alliance between its opponents and the establishment. Its uncompromising conduct today stems from what it sees as a stolen election and political manoeuvring to keep it out of power. While linked to government-opposition conflict, the second fault line is distinct: troubled relations and friction between the centre and provinces, which have punctuated the country’s history and weakened federalism. Intolerance of opposition-controlled provincial governments by parties governing at the centre became a common feature from the very inception of Pakistan. Just seven days after independence, the NWFP government was deposed, setting an unfortunate precedent. Thereafter, every province saw elected governments replaced by governor’s rule at some time or another, undermining the federation and testing the country’s unity. The consequences of intolerance of rivals together with the establishment’s efforts to centralise power and failure to make the federal arrangement work, were writ large in the rise of the Bengali nationalist movement that culminated in the break-up of Pakistan in 1971. But no lesson was learnt and the fault line endured. Fast forward to the 1990s when the regionalised nature of election outcomes meant that parties forming governments at the federal level were often different from those that constituted provincial governments. This should have urged efforts to establish smooth and cooperative centre-province relations. But that did not happen. The notion that reciprocal obligations between the centre and provinces are more than a constitutional precept and actually have to be fulfilled by both sides still finds few takers. A third fault line relates to parliament’s weakness and its inability to play its fundamental role of exercising oversight of executive actions and hold governments to account. Successive governments have viewed parliament principally as a means to maintain themselves in power rather than a forum to initiate and debate laws and policy. The preferred mode of legislating has often been through ordinance or using a brute majority to rush through laws without deliberation. This reduced parliament to little more than a rubber stamp. The most recent examples are the26thand27thConstitutional amendments that were steamrolled through parliament in 2024 and 2025 without real debate and without even sharing their texts with members before moving them. There was virtually no debate when the two chambers recently endorsed the imposition of emergency in KP. Few if any governments encouraged parliament to play an active legislative and deliberative role. Instead, they preferred the legislature to be a passive body. This remains the case. Even ruling parties with handsome majorities failed to recognise parliament’s utility as a forum to ventilate, change and share opinion. Whether this reflects lack of confidence in their backbenchers or poor understanding of how parliament should function, the outcome is marginalisation of the legislature’s role. This denudes the political system of democratic accountability. The fourth fault line — weak institutions — is no less consequential. It is rooted in a political culture that has privileged personalities over institutions, and in a ruling elite that has little appetite for strong institutions because they impose checks and balances and place limits on power. Nothing illustrates this better than the judiciary. Its independence has been steadily eroded over the years by both civilian and military governments. The recent constitutional amendments have taken this further, making the superior judiciary subservient to the executive. Political fault lines are not cast in stone. Their persistence doesn’t mean they cannot be overcome especially when their impact on the country is so damaging. But it requires bold, visionary leadership to break from the past. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: The data centre and water question
articles.content: AS plans for large data centres take shape in Pakistan, the debate has centred on jobs and investment, while a more basic concern has received little attention: water. Why would a data centre compete for water? Computing generates heat, and evaporating water is one of the most cost-effective ways to remove it. By 2030, the United Nations University projects that data centres globally will use nearly triple the combined electricity usage of Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nigeria, with an associated water footprint equal to the basic domestic needs of 1.3 billion people. In Pakistan, the per capita water availability had plummeted from 5,600 cubic metres in 1947 to roughly 930 by 2023. Some weeks ago, we argued in these pages for bringing compute to where Pakistan’s surplus electricity sits, thereby monetising capacity that consumers already pay for. Water is integral to this equation, and a deeper analysis is warranted, which we aim to provide here. How data centres keep cool: Data centres are usually cooled through open evaporative systems, which results in most of the water being lost to the atmosphere. However, these systems are comparatively cost-effective and relatively energy-efficient. Other options include closed-loop systems that recirculate water or a coolant through sealed pipes, which can cut freshwater use by up to 70 per cent; and direct-to-chip and immersion cooling, which bring liquid straight to the processor. Additionally, dry cooling uses almost no water but, by Google’s own estimate, about 10pc more energy. So there is a trade-off in cost and energy, but for a country like ours that already pays for idle generation, it is a strategic investment choice. Running the numbers: A 2016 US Department of Energy study puts average on-site data centre water use at 1.8 litres per kWh. At that rate, a 1 GW campus running continuously would consume about 16 million cubic metres a year, roughly 0.01pc of the 175 billion cubic metres the Indus supplies annually. Sky47’s 8.5MW Karakoram-01 would, based on these estimates, use around 134,000 cubic metres a year. Even accounting for Pakistan’s hotter temperatures, these figures remain marginal. Hence, nationally, data centres are not Pakistan’s water problem. Thirsty infrastructure is workable when siting follows the water. However, locally they can be. A 1 GW campus would draw about 10 million gallons a day from a single source, the same volume that Karachi’s new Rs14bn Dumlottee pipeline will add for the Defence and Clifton areas, in a city receiving 550-650 million gallons daily against a demand of around 1,200 million gallons. The burden falls on the nearest communities. Pakistan has faced this question of siting before with its nuclear power plants. Reactors with cooling towers consume about 2.5 litres per kWh, according to a 2012 review by the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory. At 6,755 GWh generated by Karachi’s K-3 unit in 2024, by the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission’s count, that’s about 17 million cubic metres a year, or about 12 million gallons a day, more than a 1 GW data centre campus. Pakistan avoided that burden through siting: K-2 and K-3 sit on the coast and cool with seawater, while Chashma draws on the Chashma-Jhelum link canal. Thirsty infrastructure is workable when siting follows the water. The problem at the foundation: Pakistan’s water crisis lies elsewhere. More than 93pc of its water goes to agriculture, and over 60pc of that is lost in conveyance and application. Four crops (rice, wheat, sugarcane, and cotton) consume over 80pc of water resources yet contribute about 5pc of GDP; Pakistan generates just $1.4 of GDP per cubic metre withdrawn, the eighth-lowest in the world. The parallel with power is striking: consumers pay for electricity that never reaches them, and the country withdraws water that never reaches a crop. The way forward: Three interventions follow: Immediate: make water a licensing condition, with energy-compute zones mandating closed-loop or dry cooling, public reporting of water use, and siting away from stressed aquifers. Dubai has promoted recycled water in district cooling since 2008, and Qatar has long incentivised non-potable cooling. Short-term: cool with wastewater. Pakistan treats barely 1pc of its collected wastewater. Meanwhile, Chennai’s tertiary treatment plants are designed to recycle a fifth of the city’s sewage for industry, and Amazon, which air-cools its Indian data centres, will use treated sewage in upcoming facilities in Mumbai and Hyderabad. Operators could co-finance similar plants in Karachi and Lahore. Long-term: reform agricultural water use. Punjab’s World Bank-backed irrigation programme improved over 15,000 watercourses while promoting drip irrigation and laser-levelling. Scaling it nationally and shifting acreage from rice and sugarcane towards pulses, vegetables, and sunflower would save water and cut edible oil imports. Saving just 1pc of the Indus water used for irrigation would supply a 1 GW campus for a century. Weighing both sides: Both sides of this debate hold part of the truth. Critics are right that a poorly sited data centre can strain a community; advocates are right that the sector will not exhaust a country. Pakistan has missed too many economic waves to let a misframed debate cost it this one. The power and water are there to support the data centre industry. What remains is the discipline to manage matters both wisely and efficiently.
articles.author: Shahzaib Saqib Warraich | Muhammad Hassan Dajana

articles.title: Ethiopian sea fever
articles.content: WITH attention sharply focused on Iran and the Saudi-Ansarullah conflict, you may be forgiven for not noticing that the East African nation of Eritrea has invaded its much larger neighbour Ethiopia. On the face of it, this is insane: Ethiopia’s population is at least 30 times that of its smaller neighbour and its GDP of $140 billion dwarfs Eritrea’s modest $2bn. In military terms, while Eritrea — thanks to its national service policy — fields a large army consisting of some 350,000 active duty soldiers and approximately 650,000 reservists, these are largely poorly armed, equipped and trained and heavily outgunned by Ethiopia, which has greatly modernised its military in recent years. Nevertheless, Eritrean forces entered Ethiopian territory in late September this year, sparking clashes with the Ethiopian army. Is Eritrea insane for taking on its much larger neighbour? Not quite. The incursion comes at a time when Ethiopia is facing an alliance of rebels that have banded together with the aim of toppling Ethiopian president Abiy Ahmed’s government. The alliance unites seven groups including the Oromo Liberation army, the Fano militia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front. The TPLF have an interesting history here; staging repeated rebellions against Ethiopian rule, the Tigrayan-led Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front actually held power in Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 when they were sidelined by the current Ethiopian leadership leading to what is known as the Tigray war of 2020-2022. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea are even more contentious: when Eritrea became independent in 1993 following a brutal 30-year conflict, it effectively cut off Ethiopia’s access to the Red Sea, something that Abiy Ahmed wants to rectify. Ethiopia and Eritrea did have a brief rapprochement during the Tigray war, when they joined forces against the TPLF. Yes, the same TPLF that Eritrea is now supporting against Ethiopia; another object lesson that while alliances are temporary, interests are permanent. Eritrea has reason to believe that if Ethiopia manages to subdue the rebels, a victorious Ethiopian army will march into Eritrea and wrest access to the Red Sea, something that Abiy deems as ‘inevitable’ and an ‘existential’ need for his country. He’s not wrong; the most populous landlocked country in the world, Ethiopia is forced to rely on the Addis-Djibouti corridor for 95 per cent of its export-import trade and has to pay close to $2bn annually in transit and port fees. Is Eritrea insane for taking on its much larger neighbour? But its rush to the Red Sea is setting off alarm bells among coastal states, notably Somalia, which is livid at Abiy’s outreach to the breakaway so-called Republic of Somaliland, that has also pledged its full support to Ethiopia’s quest for the Red Sea and is considering leasing 19 kilometres to Ethiopia. It’s worth noting that the only country to have formally recognised Somaliland is Israel, and Somaliland also has very close relations with Israel’s chief Arab ally, the UAE. Why is this important? Because while Saudi Arabia and Turkiye currently have good relations with Ethiopia, neither would be delighted to have Ethiopia formally become a littoral state of the Red Sea, and in Turkiye’s case, certainly not at the cost of Somalia, with which Turkiye has massively expanded its relations, encompassing both the military and economic spheres. For the embattled Saudis, having a state closely allied to Israel and the UAE expand its power in this manner may have negative long-term consequences. But while these are somewhat distant concerns, the expanding conflict in East Africa is certainly drawing Egypt’s attention. Why? Because Egypt, as Herodotus wrote in the 5th century BC, is “a gift of the Nile”, a saying that is as true today as it was then, and Ethiopia’s plan to build the ‘Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam’ on the headwaters of the Nile poses an existential threat to Egypt. Thus, it is in Egypt’s interests to curtail Ethiopian power as much as possible by supporting Eritrea. And then there’s Sudan, where Ethiopia is accused not only of allowing the use of its territory for arms shipments from the UAE to the rebel RSF in Sudan, but also (along with the UAE) by the Sudanese army of carrying out drone strikes on Sudanese soil. Moreover, a recent investigation by Reuters claims to have uncovered a training camp for the Rapid Support Forces in Western Ethiopia. To be fair, Ethiopia’s actions are also dictated by its financial dependence on the UAE (the RSF’s chief backer) and its fears that a victory of the Sudanese army — relations between the two have never been good — will result in a strategic encirclement of Ethiopia. And so, we see that, once again, fear and financial imperatives are stoking another conflict that will not stay confined to one region.
articles.author: Zarrar Khuhro

articles.title: Devolution deficit
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S climate challenge is a test of whether a decentralised but politically fragmented federation can govern collective risks. Climate-induced disasters do not stop at provincial boundaries. Yet institutions responsible for responding remain divided by federal-provincial tensions and ethnic and regional competition within provinces. The 18th Amendment is often portrayed as a source of fragmentation. That interpretation is incomplete. The amendment was primarily a response to excessive centralisation and provincial grievances. Its paradox is that, while it reduced vertical tensions between the centre and provinces, it did not ensure that power would travel further downward to districts and communities. The 18th Amendment addressed the imbalance by abolishing the Concurrent Legislative List. The seventh NFC Award raised the provincial share of the divisible pool from 45 to 57.5 per cent. The difficulty emerged at the next level. Provincial autonomy did not automatically produce meaningful local autonomy. Article 140A requires provinces to establish local governments (LGs) and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility and authority to elected representatives. In practice provincial political elites have often retained control over resources and decision-making. Authority has moved away from the centre without necessarily moving close enough to citizens, who experience climate risks most directly. This matters because climate governance depends on coordination at multiple levels that requires national forecasting and financing, provincial planning and district-level preparedness. Without empowered local institutions, climate policy remains concentrated in provincial capitals, where political priorities may compete and implementation capacity is weakest at the point of delivery. Intra-provincial tensions add another layer of difficulty. In Sindh, concentration of political and administrative authority in Karachi and the PPP’s dominance have contributed to a sharp urban-rural divide. In Punjab, perceptions of financial and administrative dominance by Lahore have sustained grievances in the Seraiki belt with demands for a separate south Punjab province. In KP, the renaming of the province as part of the 18th Amendment settlement generated resistance in the Hindko-speaking Hazara region and renewed demands for a separate province. These conflicts shape who controls development funds, infrastructure, public services and political representation — all central to climate resilience. Climate change demands more than a simple division of federal powers. The centre also faces constraints. Federal policymakers have argued that the post-18th Amendment fiscal settlement limits resources available for national responsibilities. Provinces, in turn, regard attempts to dilute their fiscal or legislative autonomy as a threat to constitutional guarantees. Pakistan needs national standards, shared data, coordinated disaster response, climate finance, international reporting and the capacity to meet commitments under global climate agreements. Provinces need meaningful authority over sectors affecting adaptation and resilience. Climate change, therefore, exposes the limits of treating federalism as a simple division of powers. Pakistan requires a system in which autonomy and coordination reinforce each other. The 18th Amendment should not be blamed for ethnic polarisation; rather, its unfinished devolution agenda should be addressed. Provincial governments need to make Article 140A meaningful by transferring predictable finances, administrative authority, and decision-making powers to elected LGs. Federal and provincial institutions also need permanent mechanisms for joint climate planning, shared information, disaster preparedness, and financing, while en-suring that vulnerable regions and communities have a genuine voice. The 18th Amendment is not the primary driver of ethnic divisions. However, the failure of regional ruling parties to pass these fruits down via local body governance has transformed old centre-province animosities into localised, intra-provincial ethnic fracturing. The root causes of the recent developments in KP can partly be linked to 16 years of uneven development exacerbated by political miscalculations and exploited by vested interest groups. This trend can lead to deeper alienation without local body governance. The real challenge is to prevent decentralisation from ending at provincial capitals. Climate adaptation cannot remain trapped in federal-provincial bargaining or intra-provincial ethnic competition. A resilient federation must combine autonomy with empowered LGs, cooperation and equitable access to climate resources for all its citizens.
articles.author: Aisha Khan

articles.title: Eating grass for AI
articles.content: “WE will eat grass or leaves, even go hungry, but we will get one of our own … We have no other choice!” Zulfikar Ali Bhutto had famously remarked as he voiced this nation’s determination to build an indigenous nuclear deterrent programme that had, by the mid-1960s, become an existential necessity. Some seven years later, Pakistan made it a policy imperative. That one call guaranteed the future security of the republic. Decades later, working through sheer grit and determination, Pakistan showed the world that it was more than capable of looking after itself. We stand at a very similar juncture today. The ongoing arms race in AI threatens to upend the global economic and security order, and the turning point is likely to arrive well before we will be prepared to confront it. That is, unless we once again take control of our destiny and start shaping it with our own hands today. A large part of our annual $4.6bn in IT exports is freelancing work, call centres, and entry-level coding, which modern AI directly imperils. At the rate at which the technology is progressing, it will rapidly render many of those services and products either low-value or useless. There is also the question of what we, as an economy, must pay in terms of compute bills if our companies continue to license AI usage from foreign corporations. As dependence on AI grows, the bill could reach hundreds of millions of dollars by the end of the decade. At most critical risk is our defence infrastructure, where drones, electronic warfare, and high-end sensors already run on AI technology, and are only going to grow more dependent on it to maintain their efficacy. The national leadership must, therefore, make haste. In the 1970s, Pakistan was able to offer expat talent a compelling reason to return. Similar arrangements need to be made once again. Talented computer scientists and experts from around the world must be called home, given a deadline, generous budgets, and autonomy. The systems and data centres can be placed close to where power is cheap and stable, while the research can take place where our universities are. A realistic target would be to host open-weight models at home, have researchers and technologists fine-tune them on Pakistani data and languages, run all government and defence needs within the country, and own the data pipelines as well. This would make Pakistan sovereign enough in AI without requiring a frontier-level lab or the 100-billion-dollar budgets that they need. We can build on our ambitions once the basics are in place. The Chagai test took more than two decades; the clock on AI runs much faster than that. Pakistan cannot afford to delay this project. The downside risks are too great.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Climate exodus
articles.content: SOUTH Asia may see a vast movement of people as climate change makes parts of the region harder to live in. According to the International Organisation for Migration, as many as 40.5m people could be forced to move by 2050. The warning deserves attention for what such displacement could mean for a region already struggling with poverty, overcrowded cities, unemployment, and competition for resources. From the sinking coastlines of Bangladesh to the drought-hit districts of Pakistan, climate pressures are threatening millions of livelihoods. But it is not just the communities directly affected that will feel the impact. As farmers abandon unproductive land and families leave disaster-prone areas, towns and cities will have to accommodate growing populations. Competition for housing, employment, water and public services could make life harder for poorer communities and generate social tensions. Countries with limited resources may struggle to provide for both established residents and newcomers. The danger is particularly acute in South Asia, where weak regional cooperation could hinder a coordinated response. Climate displacement could then become another source of instability unless governments prepare for it together. The warning raises questions about how Pakistan intends to accommodate people whose homes and livelihoods become impossible to sustain. Our urban centres already struggle with inadequate housing, sanitation, transport, and job opportunities. An influx of climate-displaced families could deepen these problems. Yet migration need not mean destitution. As the IOM chief has pointed out, moving can itself be a means of adapting to climate change. Pakistan must, therefore, recognise climate mobility as a permanent consideration in development planning. Provincial and local governments need reliable information about communities likely to leave, destinations likely to receive them, and services required to support their transition. Land-use policies, affordable housing, vocational training, and access to schools and healthcare must reflect changing population patterns. Equally important is protecting the rights of displaced families, who should not lose access to documentation, education or public assistance simply because they have moved. Regional cooperation on forecasting, disaster preparedness and population movements could help countries anticipate shared pressures. The challenge is to ensure that people forced to move by climate change can rebuild their lives.
articles.author: Editorial
